content: 1. Diagnostic methods for tuberculosis (TB) in children and adolescents must ensure that systems are functional to facilitate the testing of children using gastric samples at the appropriate level of care. 2. Stool sampling is a non-invasive method that is generally easy and feasible for healthcare workers (HCWs) and caregivers, regardless of the child’s clinical condition. However, a potential limitation is that children may not be able to provide stool samples on demand, leading to delays in sample collection. 3. Raising awareness and educating caregivers about stool as a suitable sample for TB testing is crucial to improve its acceptability and implementation. 4. Stool processing is considered an acceptable procedure for laboratory technicians and is regarded as a viable alternative to sputum samples. However, studies included in a systematic review reported relatively high rates of non-determinate Xpert Ultra results (e.g., errors, invalid results, or no results), ranging from less than 1% to 10%, depending on the stool processing method used. 5. A preliminary analysis compared three centrifuge-free stool processing methods combined with Xpert Ultra: optimized sucrose flotation (OSF), simple one-step stool (SOS), and stool processing kit (SPK). The results showed similar sensitivity and specificity for Xpert Ultra across all three methods. These methods were easy to process at the reference laboratory level but were not deemed suitable for non-laboratory personnel, such as nurses or HCWs, in primary healthcare settings without laboratory access. 6. Among the three methods, the SOS method was preferred because it does not require additional equipment and is comparable to sputum processing using Xpert Ultra. The SPK is still in the prototype stage and will not be commercialized, while the OSF method is under validation, with plans to simplify it into a kit format in the near future. 7. Either of the available centrifuge-free stool processing methods may be used depending on local preferences and laboratory infrastructure. 8. Trace results are common when using Xpert Ultra for pediatric specimens, reflecting the paucibacillary nature of TB in children. For children, people living with HIV, and those being evaluated for extrapulmonary TB (EPTB), an MTB complex detected trace result is considered bacteriological confirmation of TB. However, trace results do not provide rifampicin resistance information, necessitating the collection of alternative specimens for Xpert Ultra processing in individuals with a high likelihood of drug resistance. 9. Local monitoring of specimen collection by type, diagnostic test, result, and clinical diagnosis in a TB Laboratory Register (or equivalent) is recommended. Results should be recorded in a TB Register, with age disaggregation (e.g., 0–4, 5–9, 10–14, 15–19 years) as recommended by WHO for countries with case-based electronic recording and reporting systems. 10. Integrated treatment decision algorithms may be used to diagnose pulmonary TB in children under 10 years of age with presumptive TB attending healthcare facilities. These algorithms should incorporate bacteriological confirmation whenever possible, using WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic tests and appropriate pediatric specimens (e.g., stool, nasopharyngeal aspirate, induced or expectorated sputum, or gastric aspirate). 11. New integrated treatment decision algorithms for specific populations and settings have been developed and internally validated. These algorithms are evidence-based and aim to address gaps in TB case detection in children. They will remain valid for 24 months after the publication of these guidelines, after which new evidence will be reviewed. 12. TB diagnosis in children relies on a thorough assessment of evidence derived from exposure history, clinical examination, and relevant investigations. While various algorithms and scoring systems exist, they have not been systematically evaluated. There is a need for evidence-based, practical treatment decision algorithms tailored to different settings with varying access to diagnostic tests and chest X-rays (CXR). 13. An individual participant dataset (IPD) meta-analysis was conducted to evaluate and develop evidence-based treatment decision algorithms for diagnosing pulmonary TB in children under 10 years of age. Data were sourced from geographically diverse TB high-burden countries, and seven algorithms or scoring systems were evaluated for sensitivity and specificity. 14. None of the evaluated algorithms were found to be optimal in terms of sensitivity or specificity, and the evidence was of very low certainty. The panel emphasized the importance of avoiding missed TB diagnoses in children, given the large case detection gap and the consequences of a missed diagnosis. 15. The panel decided to make a generic recommendation on the use of treatment decision algorithms and to describe newly developed algorithms for relevant subgroups and settings in the operational handbook. This approach empowers HCWs, including those in settings with limited access to diagnostic tools, to make decisions on starting TB treatment in children. 16. For children living with HIV, children with severe acute malnutrition (SAM), and infants under 1 year of age, the sensitivity and specificity of the reviewed algorithms varied widely. The panel highlighted the need for specific evidence-based treatment decision algorithms for these high-risk subgroups. 17. Integrated treatment decision algorithms allow treatment decisions to be made at more decentralized levels of care, where children generally present earlier with less severe disease and lower bacteriological confirmation rates. These algorithms play an important role at peripheral levels of the healthcare system. 18. The interim conditional recommendation will remain valid for 24 months to allow for the generation of new data, including external validation of algorithms, operational research, modeling studies, and qualitative research into feasibility and acceptability for HCWs and families.
